utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, let's verify whether the videolink is functioning well. Could the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink confirm that he can see us and that he can hear us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can see and hear you clearly. And so can the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Jeremy, if you're ready to continue your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're ready, you it start, but I'll first remind the witness. Mr. Basara, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now we finished our discussion yesterday discussing your attendance at a meeting in Kljuc on the 14th of May, 1992 at which the strategic goals were discussed. Now, you said that you missed various parts of this meeting because were -- you happened to be outside trying to stop some soldiers firing into the air. You also said that now you -- you can't remember whether you may or may not have known about the strategic goals at the time of the war. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the first strategic goal that was outlined at this meeting in Kljuc on the 14th of May, 1992 was that there must be state separation of the three national communities. Now, in paragraph 19 of your statement, D1031, you -- you say that you -- you know that the attitude of the SDS people was to have the three national communities separated, you say, so each could live in peace. So we can agree that you -- that you knew about this particular strategic goal; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wasn't aware that it was called strategic objectives. I just thought it was the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you simply understood it as a war goal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in your 2009 interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you discussed the attitude of the municipal staffs, such as deputies in the assembly, towards resettlement of the non-Serb population in Sanski Most. Now, you would agree with me that many of the SDS in Sanski Most were in favour of resettling non-Serb villagers there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is partially correct, but they were the minority. There was a small group of deputies in the assembly who were advocating that idea, for the others to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that minority, they were the persons who found themselves in the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most; yes? Persons such as Rasula, such as Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rasula was one of them who were in favour of it. Vrkes was a bit more diplomatic about all of that, and he wasn't quite as outspoken, although he, too, was probably in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that this -- this notion of separation of Serbs from the Muslim and Croat people was something that the 1st Krajina Corps communicated to all the units within the corps and that's P2874 in this case. Now, as regards the dissemination to the units of this -- this particular war goal and, indeed, the six strategic objectives, you said yesterday that this could have taken place in the battalion commands or the brigade commands. That's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you found that order in the brigade command, then in all likelihood it was the brigade command that received it, and parts of their commands and battalions may have been made aware, whereas there was only one brigade, my brigade. In other words, as regards any dissemination among the fighters themselves, at that point in time, it was an impossible thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that it was possible that dissemination could have occurred in the command of the battalions, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so. As I said, I can't assert that, but all received orders, all orders received by battalion commands are forwarded to the battalion commanders. They are made aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now there's evidence in this case that's exactly what happened in your brigade; for example, P7070, which is a military notebook of a former Intel officer in your brigade. Now I'd like to show you another military notebook that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get it corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, I'd like to show you another military notebook that is in the possession of the Prosecution that we believe belongs to someone at the command level in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31873.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, while we are not clear of who the exact individual author of this particular military notebook is, it's clear from our review that this is a contemporaneous record of events during 1992. It includes a number of diary entries which I would like to take you to now or -- a couple of which I'd like to take you to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 12 in the English? Page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record it mays May 1997, so I don't know if it's a proper representation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says on the front of -- Mr. Lukic is absolutely right, it says on the front page May 1997. As I understand it that page was provided by the persons who had handed the document to the Office of the Prosecutor. It came from AID in -- from Bosnia. The -- as I mentioned, we don't know the exact person who authored this particular war diary but what is clear is it's a contemporaneous record of events. The entries are corroborated by various other diaries that we do have in evidence, such as P7070, and there's -- clearly indications of meetings of battalion commanders in the brigades. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution position is that it is contemporaneous, although 1997 appears on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page -- yes, with -- and page 10 in the B/C/S. I'd like to focus on the right side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, we see in this military notebook on the screen before you that there is a reference to a meeting in Kljuc on the 13th of May, 1992. Various items are detailed. If we go to the next entry, the 14th of May, 1992, we see a reference to strategic goals and the first one being state separation from other two communities. And seven goals here are listed. If we can to the next page, please, in both the B/C/S and the English. And if we can focus on the left side in the B/C/S, please. Now, here we see a reference to a meeting on the 14th of May, 1992. There's a reference to General Mladic. Now it's -- it's my understanding from other evidence, Colonel Basara, that General Mladic was not actually at this meeting. But my question for you is that this, nevertheless, is information originating from General Mladic that's being relayed down the chain of command to units in your brigades; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks the document refers to cannot have anything to do with my brigade because my brigade was not in Kljuc. It has do with the Kljuc brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person writing this, writing this document, most likely came from the Kljuc Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, my -- I'll focus my question. Where we see this reference to General Mladic and we read below it: "The new territory should have geography latitude that can be successfully defended. "Displacement according to the ethnic principle is also planned." That's an example of information from General Mladic being relayed to a person in -- to persons within your units. And we can go to other entries of this diary if necessary that will show you that this is, indeed, a unit in the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm really puzzled with this document. It says we don't know who composed the document. Then it is said General Mladic was not there but this is what he said. So I really cannot comprehend properly what is going on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I don't know whether I did hear you say that this is what General Mladic said but that it's -- comes from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understood it, your representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then who said that General Mladic said this? There is no data we can verify in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you have any such questions, I agree with you that you may be very precise in the way in which Mr. Jeremy presents a document what it is, but any questions as to the content of it and how to understand it you can deal with that matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's also suggested to this witness that this is something that is ordered for his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's the difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination. You can lead the witness in the understanding of a document and it's improper to intervene at this -- in this way. And, of course, you can revisit the matter in re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy. But you may be very precise in what it is. That's a different matter that -- as to how to understand it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, assuming that this notebook does belong to a unit in the 6th Brigade, then what we see before us at this meeting on the 14th of May, 1992 is an example of a comment here which is "displacement according to the ethnic principle is also planned," a comment that appears to be attributed to General Mladic being relayed to members of a unit in the 6th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not refer to the 6th Brigade because at the top of the document we find Kljuc and the date. In other words, it is an officer who in all likelihood was a SDS member in Kljuc who wrote this. Therefore, this does not pertain to my brigade, and I cannot offer any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, so the reference to Kljuc is a reference to the meeting on -- as I understand it and the Prosecution understand it, is a reference to the meeting in Kljuc on the 14th of May, 1992 that we have discussed and that you were present at.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see the heading where it says "Kljuc," it was my understanding that it had nothing to do with the 6th Brigade but that it belonged probably to a SDS member who was part of the 6th Brigade. In other words, as I said already, I cannot accept this document or offer any comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to accept any document. It is put before you. Apparently you are not familiar with the document. Whether it's an example of one thing or another and how you interpreted it at this moment is not a matter of fact within your knowledge. Mr. Jeremy, you more or less asking for an exegesis of this document at this moment and perhaps you better move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And it may be that I return to this particular document so I'd like to MFI it for now and I would also like to -- to put on the record that this particular entry is closely corroborated by evidence that we have from -- from another diary, Dragan Karic's diary, which is P7070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 31873 receives number P7321.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was involved -- we would object to introducing this document through this witness based on the facts we just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think at this moment Mr. Jeremy asked for it to be MFI'd so whether admission is appropriate for this document through this witnesses is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the -- what would be cured after it being MFI'd. It's offered through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we hear from Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this witness [sic] has been put to the witness at this moment and for that reason it is important that we know what document was put before him. Now, whether it is a document which is admissible in evidence is a different question. We limit ourselves at this moment to the request to have it marked for identification and for a full record it's important to know at least what was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember that we MFI'd everything that was put in front of the witness, every single witness in this case. And I think that was not the procedure we had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jeremy apparently wants to give it a follow-up and during the follow-up you are free to argue whatever you want as to admissibility, or even whether it was appropriate at all to put to the witness. For this moment, it is just an administrative step. It will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence -- no. That's the last thing I should have said. It's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. P7070 is not on the list so we cannot work with that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's a P number, it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to be prepared for this, Your Honour. We don't have that document. The practice is that the documents that will be used in cross-examination have to be on the list offered as list with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honours and that's why I haven't used P7070 with this particular witness. Prosecution can't possibly put every document that it has in evidence on its witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now we can use the document that are not on the list. That was not the rule that applied to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not telling us that you never used a document which was not on your list, are you? It happened now and then, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it happens now with the Prosecution. Again, it's marked for identification, nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not that one. It's the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Then I am confusing matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have simply made a reference to a document that's already in evidence. It's not the document that I've shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's different then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's just a reference. It's clear from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, that is a -- that item is moot. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, yesterday you told us that you attended meetings of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most during 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. But I did not attend all of them. Only a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you were actually a member of the Crisis Staff, were you not, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you ten times that I was not a member of the Crisis Staff, and I think that this is unnecessary. It's unnecessary for you to ask me yet again whether I was a member of the Crisis Staff when I was not a member of the Crisis Staff and when I could not have been subordinated to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, that's the first time I've asked you that question, but I'd like to show you a few documents in connection with this that I hope with provide some clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3294. And this the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula. And if we can go to page 40 in the English, please, and 30 in the B/C/S. And if we can focus on the right-hand side of the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, I don't want to spend too much time on this, but we see a reference to a Crisis Staff meeting on the 11th of May, 1992. We see the heading, Execution of tasks assigned in previous meetings. And we see that the first point here is "Basara awaiting orders from above to become a member of the War Staff as the Crisis Staff is to be referred to until further notice." Now, Colonel Basara, seeing this entry in Rasula's diary, this entry to this Crisis Staff meeting, do you recall requesting authorisation to become a member of the Crisis Staff or of the -- of the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just a moment, please. Could you stop. [In English] It's not what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a translation issue or is that you -- let's first establish. Is there anything wrong with the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, obviously there is a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the translators could read the first sentence under one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know this is usually not the place where we verify translations but under these present circumstances, in order to avoid that we choose a path which is based on a wrong translation, could you please slowly read that first entry in your language, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I quote: "[Interpretation] Basara expects orders from above in order to enter the War Staff."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's not "become a member" but "enter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In which way he would enter, it's debatable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Jeremy, the final resolution of the language issue not being there yet, could you again put the question to the witness offering the two -- the two possible translations of that one word. And, Witness, you were not asked to comment on the word "War Staff," that was part of the question already. Carefully listen to the question as will now be phrased by Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I'll go with the version that Mr. Lukic read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, do you agree that you, at the point of 11th of May, 1992, you were awaiting orders from above to enter into the -- the War Staff, as the Crisis Staff was to be referred to until further notice. Do you agree that you were awaiting for those orders from above?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not awaiting any orders. That I know. So why Rasula wrote that, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I take it that your answer would be the same if the version was to read that you were awaiting orders to become a member of the -- the War Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Staff did not exist because a state of war had not been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's clear -- you will agree that it's clear from this entry that Rasula obviously thought that a War Staff did exist and he considered this to be the new name for the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot say. I mean, I cannot assert what it was Rasula was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I cannot comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's understood. Thank you, Colonel Basara. I've got a couple of other documents on this same topic I don't think we need to look at all of them but there's evidence in this case that at the end of this same month, May 1992, there are conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most which, again, which records you as being a member of the Crisis Staff. Now, these conclusions were on the 30th of May, 1992, so shortly after the events in Mahala. Does that prompt your recollection that you might have perhaps joined the Crisis Staff immediately after the events in Mahala in -- shortly before events in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is unnecessary, to put questions at all about the Crisis Staff because I as commander, as a professional could not have allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I have to stop you here. You may not understand but it's in fairness to you that Mr. Jeremy puts to you what is found in documentary evidence which contradicts your testimony. That's the reason why he does it and that's a good reason. Would you refrain from commenting on whether or not it's good to ask certain questions and whether it's appropriate to do it or to do it more times. We'll deal with that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, I take it that my -- my prompt about the timing of this particular conclusion on the 30th of May, 1992 indicating that you were, indeed, a member of the Crisis Staff doesn't refresh your recollection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary to refresh my recollection about the Crisis Staff. I have told you that I'm a professional soldier, a brigade commander, who did not want to place himself under the command of the civilian structures, and I did not accept that, and that is how I stayed on until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, Colonel Basara, it's correct, is it not, that you were a member of the Crisis Staff in your very capacity as a brigade commander. That's -- that's the reason -- that's the very -- an express reason that you were actually on the Crisis Staff in the first place. That's -- that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a final document in connection with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P4161.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, these are some conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. They are dated the 19th of June, 1992. And we see they're conclusions from a meeting on the 18th of June 1992. Now, we see that there are lists of two -- two sets of names. The first set are permanent members of the Crisis Staff and we see number 7, Branko Basara. Now, we see this list of what looks like two tiers of responsibility of persons in the municipality and you're in the first list, the permanent list. So does the permanence of your role within the Crisis Staff, does that perhaps refresh your recollection that you were, indeed, a member?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not any kind of member of the Crisis Staff. Why they wrote my name down there, I have no idea. Probably because I attended certain meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a different topic. Now, I'd like to discuss your relationship with the -- with the civilian police. Now as brigade commander, you regularly met with the chief of police, Mirko Vrucinic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not regularly. When necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's explore that a little bit. Now, Mirko Vrucinic was actually your chief of intelligence in the 6th Brigade while you were in Jasenovac. That's -- that's true; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And for a short period of time, he -- he continued to be your chief of intelligence after your brigade was transferred to Sanski Most on the 3rd of April, 1992. That's also correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you knew one another well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Nedjeljko Rasula requested that Vrucinic be reassigned from your units -- from your brigade to the head of the MUP in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretary for National Defence asked, and he is in charge of manning the brigade and manning the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked about this during the Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, you -- you stated that it -- it was Nedjeljko Rasula who requested that Vrucinic be police commander in Sanski Most. Does that -- was that answer correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked the secretary. In fact, he asked his own organ and then that organ asked me for approval to have Vrucinic appointed chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Thank you. Now you considered Mirko Vrucinic to be very skilled at his job; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you therefore co-operated well; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had good co-operation when necessary. Not regularly, as you had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it was necessary for you to have this good co-operation during, for example, military operations that your brigade was engaged in within Sanski Most. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-operation was mainly through security organs. They collected information about Muslims and Croats who had weapons. That is where most of the co-operation took place. As for some operations, there was no co-operation there whatsoever. We did not carry out certain actions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And those actions were, for example, actions in Mahala, Hrustovo and Vrhpolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did you carry out any disarming operations with the civilian military in, for example, Mahala at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's have a quick look at a document, please, in connection ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you are recorded - and that's what I think I heard - to have spoken about the civilian military. Could you please rephrase that question, seek an answer again, and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, my question for you is whether Mirko Vrucinic and his civilian police carried out any disarming operations in co-operation with your brigade in, for example, Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did not discuss disarming in Mahala with anyone. I had enough information. Mahala is small, in terms of territory. That is to say, it is a neighbourhood. I thought that I had enough men in order to check things out and to disarm people. If there is some co-operation, then the co-operation is in terms of information as to who has weapons so that they could be taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness at this point in time. Mr. Basara, a moment ago, you said, "we carried out certain actions together." Co-operation in exchanging - wait a moment, please. Co-operation in exchanging information is one thing, but you said certain actions. Which kind of actions did you carry out together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that we were carrying out actions together because I had enough forces to act independently and that has to do with disarmament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they, along parallel lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll verify what you said on the basis of the audio, whether you said that you carried out -- that you were involved in actions together. We'll try to have that done as soon as possible. But you're now saying that you were not co-operating in action? Mr. Lukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first, we should ask the witness whether the witness understands any English because I don't know exactly what is audible at the other side. Witness, could you tell us whether you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I studied French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll not speak French. Could you please take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Lukic, you're instructed not to speak French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm on the safe side. I don't speak French unlike you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness what we heard said "nismo," which means we were not. And it was translated "mi smo," we were. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the exact page and line reference so that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it was recorded that he said we carried out, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is page 19, line 25. Page 18, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It says we carried out certain actions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have that verified, Mr. Lukic, and as you know you're always welcome if there's any problem in terms of translation or interpretation or transcription. I ... Could the witness be invited to put on his headphones again. We'll continue. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, as I understand it, it's your position that the 6th Brigade did not co-operate with the civilian police with the SJB in -- in any disarming operations in Sanski Most. Is that -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-operation that was carried out, as I've already said, for collecting information. Together -- the units and the MUP did not act together anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So not co-operation for the purpose of disarming; is that -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carrying out actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My question is just to clarify your answer. You're saying that you did not co-operate with the SJB in any disarming operations in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of co-operation you mean. Do explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, there may be a little problem. You asked whether there was co-operation. Earlier the witness said there was co-operation but limited to intelligence. Now, if you ask him again whether there was any co-operation, the witness is still in doubt as to what kind of co-operation. Do I take it that are you asking the witness whether there was any co-operation in the field during such operations? Is that what you intend to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, any co-operation in the course of disarming actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- Witness, you've heard the question. That is, whether it's your position that there was never any co-operation between your brigade and the civilian police during disarming operations. That means co-operation in the field. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not co-operate because I, as commander, when I planned and organised activities, I did not involve the MUP. Now, whether some of them, somewhere, got involved without any agreement having been reached on that, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Basara, given your close relationship with Mirko Vrucinic, how likely is it that members of his police force would have been involved in operations together with members of your brigade that you were not aware of? It's not very likely, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have happened only in the case of individuals who could, together with their neighbours or relatives, become involved. However, the civilian police was never involved to resolve this in the field together with the brigade. Except for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- your position is clear. So how about the Territorial Defence? They were -- they were involved in disarming operations together with the 6th Brigade; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, they were not under my command, and they did not do that. If they did that, they could have on orders from the Crisis Staff along parallel lines, for example, while we are disarming one village, at that time they could have been disarming another village because I know where I issued orders, which villages I had disarmed and it wasn't all villages. So the last one was Hrustovo. If necessary, I can enumerate the villages that we disarmed, the 6th Brigade. And the other villages were probably disarmed by somebody who was not the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They acted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And, again, we didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the -- the -- your last -- could you repeat the last sentence of your last answer, please, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never organised together with the Territorial Defence. That is to say, if disarming took place in villages and if the brigade was not involved, then it was the TO and the police that did that. So I can enumerate the villages where the 6th Brigade carried out the disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we have a look at one document in connection with this, P2889.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, just very quickly before the break, what's coming up on the screen before you is a -- it's a report on the process of disarming military formations in the Sanski Most public security station area, and it's dated the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page, please, in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see it's signed by a Mirko Vrucinic. And if we can just go back to the first page, I just want to focus your attention on the first paragraph, and I should indicate this is a report that's being sent to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Ministry of Interior Banja Luka Security Services Centre. Colonel Basara, in the first paragraph we read that: "Serbian army units of and commands (six brigades), Territorial Defence units and the SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most municipal area." So, sir, it's very clear that Mirko Vrucinic considered the SJB, the civilian police, to be co-operating with the 6th Brigade and with the Territorial Defence in disarming operations in Sanski Most. Is it your position that he is -- that he's incorrect in -- in stating this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. One second, Witness. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do we can see co-operation? [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- you misrepresented the evidence, the document in your question to the witness. It says that army units and commands, TO, and SJB have for sometime been disarming, paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. That's my mistake and I got ahead of myself. I apologise to the Chamber and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, Colonel Basara, let me read that sentence to you again. It reads: "Serbian army units and commands (six brigades), TO Territorial Defence units and the SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most municipal area." Now, my question for you is that this is clearly an indication of co-operation between those different entities within the Sanski Most in the disarming process; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the way you formulated it. Everybody did their own part of work and then, at the end, it resulted in the implementation of disarming. However, this does not indicate any co-operation. I've already explained what that co-operation entailed, which was gathering intelligence, gathering data. However, there was no other co-operation. The brigade independently carried out the disarming process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So do I understand your position to be that it is true that the 6th Brigade was involved in disarming, the TO was involved in disarming, and the civilian police were involved in disarming, but they were doing this individually and they weren't co-operating and the only way that they did co-operate was to share information. That's your position; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before we would take a break, I have one question. How was it avoided that suddenly TO, SJB and one of the brigades would appear at the same village in order to disarm it? And how was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in what village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm -- what I'm suggesting to you is there may have been some co-ordination, TO goes here, SJB goes there, a brigade goes there, so as to have all the villages disarmed in such a way that no one was left out and that everyone that did - although individually and in its own responsibility - did the disarming in the villages they were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with their plan in terms of the security services and Territorial Defence. I was not informed by anyone about their activities. I only know what I planned and which villages I disarmed. The last one was Hrustovo. So Mahala and Hrustovo. The other villages adjacent to Sanski Most are the villages I did not disarm. They had already been disarmed by the TO and security services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you knew that they had been disarmed by the TO and the security service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I received such information that they had carried out disarming, but they never informed me about what they were doing. My security organs forwarded information to me to the effect that some villages had been disarmed by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was a lucky coincidence that did you not appear at the same village early in the morning, TO, SJB, and the army in order to disarm that village. It was coincidence, or was there any co-ordination as to, You go there on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As regards Mahala, the information we had was that the Muslims there were organised and that it could only be carried out by the 6th Brigade. There was expectation of encountering resistance, as was the case in the end. The same goes for Hrustovo. As for the other villages close to Sanski Most, we did not have such information and thus the 6th Brigade was not involved. Once the brigades was finished with its activities there may have been others coming to that village to carry out checks, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is this the kind of intelligence information you shared which made it possible that the needs for disarming were such that it would be either your brigade or the TO or the SJB that effectively could carry out such disarming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I received my orders from the corps command, as the commander in charge, I assessed the situation in the territory based on the information I had received, and I assessed which villages were supposed to be disarmed by our forces. All villages between Lusci Palanka and Sanski Most were the villages we controlled, and there were no armed conflicts in any of them. They co-operated, thanks to me touring those villages and taking measures. As for the other villages close to Sanski Most, as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm interrupting you. You go far beyond what I asked you. It was time for a break already ten minutes go. Apologies for that. We take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'll first verify whether the videolink is functioning well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours. We can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The same is true for this side. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I would like to stay with this same issue of co-operation with the TO and the police in Sanski Most, and actually, I'll focus on your co-operation with Anicic within the TO. Could we please see D00079. And, Colonel Basara, I'll tell you as it is coming up, these are conclusions of a Crisis Staff meeting from the 22nd of May. The conclusions are dated the 22nd of May and the meeting itself was on the 21st of May, 1992. So we see there the heading, "Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most," we see the date the 22nd of May, and we see the heading, "Conclusions" and then there's two conclusions below there. If we could go to page 2 in the English, please, and page 3 in the B/C/S. Now, Colonel, I'd like to focus your attention on paragraph 4 where we read as follows: "As far as disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most is concerned, Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic are charged with putting this into practice." So, Colonel Basara, in the process of putting these disarming operations into practice, you co-operated with Colonel Anicic who was then the head of the TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not even aware of the fact that Colonel Anicic was the TO commander. This does not indicate in any way that the two of us co-operated in -- on this matter. It is stated that Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic are in charge, meaning that Basara was responsible for his share of work and Anicic was probably responsible for some tasks given to him by the municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall sitting in meetings with Colonel Anicic with Mirko Vrucinic during this period, planning disarming operations in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. I did attend the meetings and most of them were also attended by Colonel Anicic who kept the minutes and attendance. I thought he a recording clerk in the municipality, as Vrucinic used to be. In other words, I do not remember us discussing it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, you do recall being in meetings with Colonel Anicic but your understanding was this former JNA colonel was basically there to take the minutes of the meetings. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding of his role.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So did he talk in these meetings or he was only there in a silent capacity, taking notes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was silent most of the time. Sometimes he would nod when Rasula spoke. As I said, my understanding was that he did not play any major role. That he was there as a kind of recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay, that's clear. Let's take a look at one of those -- the minutes of one of those meetings to see if they shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we remove this document, can we see the previous page, please. I -- okay. I was just looking at this subparagraph (d) and wanted to find out from the witness, if you can, Witness, it is said that here that: "The commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Basara, and the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence, Colonel Anicic, are hereby instructed to protect vital facilities in the town, above all the water supply system, the transformer station, the silo, et cetera." Did you two at least co-operate with each other with respect to this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not co-operate on this. I was not in charge of securing those facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards these conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's wait for the next question, Witness. If at the very end there is something you would like to add, you will have an opportunity do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm done, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And as a follow-up to His Honour Moloto's question, I'd like to take a look at the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula, which we were just looking at, and if we go to page 51 in the English and 36 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, we'll need the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive me. P3294.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, what will be coming up are actually the minutes of the meeting on 21st of May, 1992 that the conclusions that we just looked at refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 51 in the English and page 36 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there minutes of note about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: They're the minutes of the meeting and the document we just looked at contains the conclusions from the meeting that we're now going to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. Earlier you announced that we would look at some of the meetings; that's what we are doing now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you are talking about minutes. I consider usually minutes to be more or less verbatim reports which this seems not to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. So -- notes on the meeting and then notes recorded in Nedjeljko Rasula's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 36 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And focussing attention on the right-hand side of the page, we see a Crisis Staff meeting dated 21st of May, 1992. We see a reference to Colonel Basara. We see that you're talking about issues relating to the TO Staff, that the TO has been -- number 2: "The TO Defence has been given the status of an army under a single command." If we can go to the next page in each language, please. Focussing on the left side, there we see a reference under item 2 to Colonel Anicic, he is talking about work organisation and switching to war-time production. Then we see this reference to securing vital facilities, water reservoirs, Velprom. Security plans to be drawn up by Colonels Basara and Anicic. So, Colonel Basara, looking at the minutes of this meeting you attended, does that help to refresh your recollection about your discussions to secure these facilities, facilities that we saw referred to in the conclusions of the Crisis Staff dated the next day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in any way in the creation of these conclusions. I'm not familiar with them whatsoever. At the bottom, just beneath the conclusions, it doesn't say who those conclusions were supposed to be forwarded to. They were supposed to be sent to those who were expected to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps I've confused you. What we're looking at now is the record of the meeting as written by Nedjeljko Rasula and he's recording -- the assumption is that he is recording what was said at that meeting and one of the things that was said at that meeting was that you, Colonel Basara, and Anicic would secure certain vital facilities and we see reference to water reservoirs and Velprom. Does that refresh your recollection about your discussion --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to recollect. I did not devise any plan with Anicic, so I don't know whether this reflects some idea of his that he noted down. I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right, let's look at item 3 where we see a reference to Mirko Vrucinic, the police commander. "Colonel Basara and Mirko to negotiate disarmament arrangements with Sabic, first in Kamengrad and then in town." So this suggests that you are co-ordinating with Mirko Vrucinic in the course of disarmament arrangements in Sanski Most, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. It does not confirm I was involved in it because I did not accept orders or suggestions from the Crisis Staff or municipal bodies. It was their wish, but I did not implement it together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. But -- before we leave this diary, let's take look at one more entry along a similar line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we stay with this page at the moment. Some lines down, Mr. Basara, I read your name again, and I quote: "Colonel Basara: Do not confiscate weapons for which they own a licence but carry out inspections and issue new licences." Do you remember this meeting where you urged the people not to confiscate weapons for which the people have their own licence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I think you might need to scroll to the right in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Let's move to the right side of the B/C/S page. Can you see that, what I read to you? I think it's on top of that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the initial variant when a deadline was issued for the hand-over of weapons. So the weapons were not seized but it was suggested that they be called upon to hand over their weapons. What we had in mind was military, were military weapons, automatic rifles and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can I take it from your answer that you remember having been at this meeting where Mr. Rasula has taken these notes from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rasula kept the notes. I don't remember this specifically. I only know what I proposed, and based on what I have just read, I realised that it was my suggestion, that it be handled this way during disarming. I don't know, though, when exactly it took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you confirm that Mr. Rasula quoted you correctly when he noted down your words; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Overall, it does reflect the gist of it, but I don't know whether he recorded it precisely as I put it. I was just speaking and he put it down in shorthand, so to speak, because if I remember, my address was longer than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one or two questions to you, Witness. A few lines further down, Mr. Rasula's diary records that Colonel Anicic is talking. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read it for yourself - not aloud but just for yourself - and tell me when you've read that portion. It's in the middle of your page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you remember that Colonel Anicic addressed these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what is recorded here by Mr. Rasula doesn't give the impression that Mr. Anicic is there as a note-taker, but that he's, rather, participating in the discussions at the meeting fully. Do you agree with that, or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree because Rasula could have written this on the basis of his conversation in the office and then he proposed it to him as he was noting it down. Hence, I don't remember it, and I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would expect Mr. Rasula to include in his notes from meetings just private conversations he would have outside that meeting and then not clearly indicate that? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you should understand it that way. I think he wrote down what he thought was necessary. So in all likelihood, he just wrote it. That's all I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we'll shortly move away from this diary, but I'd like to look at one final entry on page 56 in the English, please, and page 40 in the B/C/S. Now, Colonel Basara, on the screen before you and if we can look at the left side in the B/C/S, is another entry in Rasula's diary of a -- another Crisis Staff meeting. It's dated 24th May 1992. We see item 2, we see a briefing given by Mirko Vrucinic. He's referring to increasing security at various locations. Point (c), control of the silo - "how we can capture it. "Colonel Basara will secure the silo." Then we look at item 3, reference to: "The operation being successful so far only in the case of weapons belonging to the TO and the republican police, while nothing has been done about weapons from illegal sources." We see a reference to, Colonel Basara proposed a strike at the strongest points [sic]. We see Colonel Anicic suggested various locations. If we go to the next page in the English, please. And we see a reference to: "Could Colonel Basara will prepare an operation against Demisevci, evening. The proposal was not accepted. It was decided that it should take place on Tuesday ..." Colonel Basara, this is a clear indication of discussions and co-ordination between Mirko Vrucinic, between Colonel Anicic, and yourself in preparation for what were then ongoing disarming operations in Sanski Most, correct, these aren't notes by Colonel Rasula of private conversations that he had outside of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any private conversations in mind. As they say, he was simply doing something of his own accord, noting down what he wanted to. This does not indicate that the brigade was engaged whatsoever. If there were any proposals to that effect, in all likelihood I never accepted them. I have no knowledge about this. I just know that we were not engaged in the operation concerning Demisevci in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you doubt that you were at this meeting, having these discussions with Colonel Anicic and Mirko Vrucinic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing an attack on Demisevci in any way. We probably did speak at some other meetings, but not about Demisevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the witness tell us what he meant when he said "we"? Who discussed? Witness, could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "we," some names were mentioned, and that's what I had in mind. I said that we could have discussed some other issues at some other locations or on a different day. But as regards Demisevci, I know I did not discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just asked who "we" are. You gave a bit of a vague answer. Some names were mentioned. Do you mean Anicic, Vrucinic, Rasula included as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I said that I did have the names in mind. They were referred to, and I said "we." "We" may have discussed it but I don't remember when or what about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when you say "we," you refer to then, that is Anicic and Vrucinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I had the two in mind. Because there was a reference about us discussing something. However, I do not remember us discussing this problem mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anicic being the note-taker with whom you discussed these kind of matters. Is that properly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not discuss it with him. Please do not turn things around. I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well, I asked you who you meant when you were talking about "we" and you confirmed that at least Anicic and Vrucinic were among those you had on your mind. I'm not twisting your words. I'm inviting Mr. Jeremy to put his next question to you. No, please wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'll actually move to a different document which is related to this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31873, and that's the war diary that we looked at at the start of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's P7321, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And could we please go to page 19 in the English and 14 in the B/C/S. And if we can focus on the left-hand side of the page in the B/C/S to begin with, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, this is an entry in this notebook that we were looking at earlier. It's dated 25th of May, 1992 which is the same date as the entry in Rasula's diary that we looked at a moment ago. We see a number of items. First item --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you apparently interrupted Mr. Jeremy. Your words were not heard. If there's anything to be said, wait until he has finished his question and then answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, I just want to take you to a few items that we see listed on the 25th of May, 1992. We see a reference to confiscation of weapons by force, "take weapons during the night (early in the morning). Number 1: "Bring out all weapons within one hour (all, both legal and illegal)." We see number 2: "Let them evacuate women and children (if they do not hand over the weapons)." Now, at point 8 we see the order and we see reference to: "Start with Skucani Vakuf and then go on (Gorice, Naprelje, Okrec)." If we could go to the next page, please, or scroll over to the right in the B/C/S. Now we see what looks like planning for the operation. "Tomorrow, day one completion up to and including, Suhaca. Day 2, we push on to Demisevci." Skipping down, we see Mahala is to be blocked. We see reference to further Mahala, Kruhari, Trnova, Sehovci, Poljak. I see a reference to Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. And below that we see a reference to "Be ready at 0600, and open fire at Demisevci. Now, Colonel, this reflects planning for the disarming operations that the 6th Brigade were involved in in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your view, then, what do these entries reflect if not planning for operations against the locations listed here, including Demisevci which we see -- saw a reference to in Rasula's diary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that what is mentioned up here, Okrec and the other villages, those villages were checked by the 6th Brigade, that is to say all of them, Fajtovci, Okreci, Skucani Vakuf, Kamengrad and so on. All of that was dealt with by the 6th Brigade on their own. No one was arrested. No force was applied. No violence, nothing. Mahala also the 6th Brigade. As for this plan that you are presenting to me, it is totally unknown to me, I don't know who made that plan, and that -- on the basis of that somebody acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say on the basis of that, someone acted. So we see this reference to Mahala, the plan for the -- this entry is dated the 25th. Now it's correct, isn't it, that your forces and you personally acted against Mahala on the 26th of May, 1992. You were involved in a military operation there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can call it whatever you want, military operation. But we actually set out to check things and to take weapons away. Fire was opened and afterwards, the soldiers continued, that is to say, launched an attack and Mahala was taken. However.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- three hours were given to get all of those out who --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... shortly. I have one final question on this entry. We see a couple of references to Demisevci. Now, we saw a reference to that location in Rasula's diary entry, which was the same date, and you say you don't recall discussing the location of Demisevci. Seeing it referred to here in the diary of a member of your brigade, does that refresh your recollection that you did indeed have discussions about that location with Rasula, Anicic, and Vrucinic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please prove that to me, that that is a member of my brigade who made this plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether this refreshes your recollection. And apparently it does not. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the question we have, "in the diary of a member of your brigade." Where we can find that, please. Finally, for the tenth time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, do you want to say something more about the document so as to give support to the Prosecution's position in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Firstly, that the Prosecution is entitled to put the witness their position in respect to this diary. And I've put to the witness that's it's our position that it belongs to a member of his brigade. In terms of the content of the diary, while we are not clear who the original author of the diary is, it is clearly a contemporaneous record of events that occurred in Sanski Most and as we've just seen from the previous exhibit that we were looking at, it's corroborated by other evidence in this case including that exhibit and a number of other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know where it was found?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It was handed over to -- it was -- it was located by AID in Bosnia, I understand after the war and handed over to the -- to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it if you have not located it you can't hand it over. That's pretty clear but my question was do you know where it was found, prior to it being given to OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My understanding it was found in an empty house in -- in Bosnia in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has drawn your attention to the question or to your supposition that you said, "in the diary of a member of your brigade." What is the basis of this assumption that it was written by a member of the brigade of Mr. Basara?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, the basis of that assumption is the entries reflect planning of operations that evidence in this case suggests that the brigade was involved in, for example, the attack on Mahala that we saw referenced in Rasula's diary that we see referenced in this diary and that we know occurred on the 26th of May 1992. The entries are also corroborated by another diary, the diary of Dragan Karic, P7070, and the very close corroboration between, for example, the entry on the 14th of May in this diary and the entry on the 14th of May in Dragan Karic's diary, that's page 4 of P7070. So, our position is even though the author of this diary is not clear, that is ultimately an issue of weight to be afforded to the diary. But there is no doubt it is an authentic contemporaneous account of events as occurring in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution of the Prosecution that the author was a member of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The basis for what is the reference to the various military operations that are recounted throughout the diary. Military operations that the 6th Brigade were involved in within Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, quite the opposite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Basara explained that they did not take part in those operations. Secondly, where is the proof that this is -- that this diary is made at the time? We just heard now that it was received from AID. AID was not only accused of forgeries but also of terrorism. So, please, and my learned friend should inform the witness that this was their position, that it was made by a member of his brigade, not to ask the witness this -- this was made by the member of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to introduction of any document received from AID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw it from Trnovo, the forgeries made by them. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on at this moment. It may take quite a bit of analysis before the Chamber could decide whether or not this document has probative value or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course. Meanwhile, Mr. Jeremy, would you be very cautious in making a clear distinction between what stands for a fact and what is an inference drawn by the examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, can you think of who else other than someone in your brigade would be writing down detail about operations that your brigade were involved in, in preparation for disarming, on operations in Sanski Most. And, in particular, why someone on the 25th of May would be referring to attacks against Mahala, attacks against Vrhpolje and Hrustovo that we know transpired a few days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the proof that this was written on 25th of May, not after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an objection. But I invited Mr. Jeremy to clearly state what your position is and that is, here, that the Prosecution assumes that this was written at that time. And you're asking whether the witness would have any idea as to who else could have written such details about the operations which were conducted at the time as indicated in this document? That's what you wanted to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, then, Witness, I don't know whether you wanted to hear the question again. It will then be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that was written up here, it could have been written up by anybody from the Crisis Staff or the municipality or the Territorial Defence. As for what is said here that the 6th Brigade took part in the action vis-à-vis Mahala, that was my personal plan, and it has nothing whatsoever to do anything with this. So the brigade independently planned disarming. All the villages along the road Lusci Palanka, Sanski Most. I assume that the Prosecutor knows that. Mahala and Hrustovo too. All the other villages, the brigade did not plan that at all and the brigade did not take part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's stay with the subject of Mahala, Colonel Basara. Now Mahala was a -- a Muslim area of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And on the 26th of May, 1992, residents there were given a three-hour warning to evacuate, after which units from your brigade shelled Mahala. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that way. What was said was that all of those who don't want to fight should get out of Mahala. That is to say, only those who wished to put up resistance and fight are to stay in Mahala. That is the truth. As for the rest that you phrased within your question, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So those who did not wish to fight were given a three-hour warning to evacuate Mahala after which it was shelled. That's your answer; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not shelled. When the soldiers went to Mahala, a few shells from a mortar fell within the line. Later on, we found that 60-millimetre mortar in Mahala. And so they opened that mortar and that's when fire was opened at Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So units from your brigade did, indeed, shell Mahala. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said to you just now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound is no longer good enough for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. We do understand that the quality of the audio is not good at this moment. I think the experience of the last few days was that this sometimes changes very quickly again. So I filled 20 seconds. Let's give it another try and see whether the quality is now better. Could you again put your question to the witness, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, my understanding is that your position is that units from your brigade did shell Mahala; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
