utterances.text: I said to you how it was that the shelling took place. You cannot take things out of context, just saying yes or no. So, first, three hours were given for all of those do not want to fight to get out, to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm interrupting you. You've explained that to us. And Mr. Jeremy finally then sought confirmation that your units, perhaps with the whole history as you explained it to us, finally fired shells at Mahala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fighting took place, and during combat, both were firing. So it wasn't just random shelling of a peaceful settlement. Rather, combat activities were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including firing shells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, firing projectiles, it is only natural in armed combat, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, you know that civilians in Mahala died as a consequence of this military operation. You know that; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to discuss the involvement of your Chief of Staff in relation to Mahala. Your Chief of Staff was Major Veljko Brajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I didn't see a reference to this in your statement, but you've previously admitted that you -- you know that your Chief of Staff ordered the destruction of a mosque in Mahala. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my doubts. I did not claim anything. I had my doubts. I thought that he couldn't have done that, but later on I found it was the commander of the SOS, Njunja, that destroyed that. I mean, he didn't need to take orders. He just did what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. No one asked you at this moment what happened. What Mr. Jeremy asked you is whether you had previously admitted that you knew that your Chief of Staff ordered the destruction of a mosque. Did you say that in -- previously?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had my doubts, that I doubt that he could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you say today, or is what you said previously? Because that is what the question was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had my doubts. Now I don't know exactly what that was I said at some point before, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... then we'll ask Mr. Jeremy to move on and he may have recordings of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And just another question on this. You previously said that not only did Veljko Brajic order the destruction of the mosque in Mahala but that he actually destroyed the mosque in Mahala, the mosque was destroyed pursuant to his order. That's what you've previously said; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at your interview in 2002, your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. After than we'll take a look at your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 27968. And if we can go to page 107 in the English and we have a B/C/S translation at page 133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Jeremy, I'd like to come back just for a second to an issue that arose earlier today, that is, whether the witness said that "we carried out certain actions together," CLSS, that is the Conference and Language Services Section, has verified on the basis of the audio and reports that what the witness said is "we did not carry it out -- carry out certain actions together." Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for drawing our attention to this issue. It has been verified. Witness, you may remember the dispute on what you said before it has been verified and you said indeed you did not carry out actions together. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, I'd like you to focus on the screen on the left -- on the document on the left side and we see the -- we see that you are asked about the destruction of a -- we see that you are asked -- I'm just finding the reference in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It can't be the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we need to go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So halfway down the page, and it's at line 12 in -- in the B/C/S, we read that you state: "I know of a mosque in Sanski Most. The Chief of Staff ordered it the Chief of Staff Brajic Nedjeljko ordered that mosque to be destroyed when he was the chief of the engineers." "Q. Your Chief of Staff? "Branko Basara: Yes. At the time that the attack on Mahala happened. "Q. He ordered the destruction of the mosque. "A. He ordered that the mosque be demolished." So, Colonel Basara, does this refresh your recollection that in 2002 you did, indeed, tell -- you did, indeed, state that your Chief of Staff destroyed the mosque in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not destroy that mosque. Later on, I found out that he had ordered the chief of engineers to do that. However, in the meantime Njunja did that, the commander of the SOS. So his order was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say that later on you found out that Njunja was responsible, so this was after you gave this answer in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I found out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. Later on you found out. When -- when was that? Was after this interview in 2002?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, people come from those parts. I can't remember who it was that I talked to exactly. And one man said that he knows with 100 per cent certainty that Njunja destroyed that mosque and he was the only one who was in the area of Sanski Most who could handle explosives properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I have limited time. My question is: When did you find this out? When were you told that Njunja destroyed this mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime later, after I had conversations and provided statements. Then I met some people from the area of Sanski Most and we talked about it all. Then one of them told me that he was positive that it was done by Njunja and that the chief of engineers should not be charged with that because he didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- let me try and get a time-frame for this. Did you find out this information before 2009?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say what year it was when I learnt that. No idea. I just know that I had those conversations, that I was in contact with the people coming in, and we started remembering things. That is how I remember one of them told me that it was Njunja. That whenever explosives were used and mosques were involved, it was his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to just quickly to go to what you said during your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case in 2009 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do that -- Could the witness tell us who it was that told you that Njunja did it? Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, how could I remember? I spoke to so many people. I can't remember who told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you. You've answered my question, Witness. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I will ask for this -- this page to be -- this page of this interview to be tendered. I'm happy to come back to these pages [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll reserve a number for it but this page then should be uploaded separately. Madam Registrar, the number would be reserved for an excerpt from the interview with Mr. Basara would receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, number would be P7322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to 65 ter 31876. I'd like to go to page 77. And this is the testimony of Branko Basara in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, there isn't a translation of this so you'll need to listen to my words carefully, but I'm going to read you the questions and answers that you provided during your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we scroll down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, focussing on line 18, we read as follows: "Q. Sorry, do you mean that you did make the request to General Talic, that Major Brajic who had confessed to blowing up a mosque should be removed? And I mean in June not in December" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You shouldn't read too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "I didn't only refer to the mosque issue, but also his work and his conduct as my first assistant, and I had insisted a few times in conversations with the General Talic that he be removed from the brigade. "Q. Right. Did you say to General Talic who also incidentally issued an order, didn't he, that mosques should not be destroyed or other religious documents, did you explain to General Talic that he had confessed to blowing up a mosque and, therefore, should be dismissed? "A. I conveyed this to General Talic, and most probably in the end he did accept my request to remove him from the brigade because I was afraid if he did stay in the brigade." So, Colonel Basara, it's clear that when you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case on the 13th of October, 2009, it was clear in your mind that Major Brajic was indeed responsible for the destruction of this mosque; yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the text and following those statements, I am quite surprised to see it there. I know why I went to see General Talic, asking him that Brajic and I leave the brigade together, that we both leave. It was because Brajic tried to split up the brigades between his and my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to take over control of the brigades at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir my simple question to you is the follows [sic]: It's clear that when you testified in Stanisic and Zupljanin case on the 13th of October, 2009 it was clear in your mind that Major Brajic was responsible for the destruction of this mosque. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, concerning the mosque, I was unable to establish anything but I did receive some information that Njunja did it. Because Brajic did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I stop you again. You apparently consider it important to give us your thoughts of today. You've given them already. Mr. Jeremy asked you whether, when you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, whether you testified as he read it to you and which clearly expresses your conviction at that time, that Major Brajic was responsible for the destruction of the mosques. Is that what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not my conviction. I was only wondering or I was in doubt if it was he who could have issued the orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what is expressed or what is recorded as would -- what you said at the time. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would. But I had no proof. And I couldn't assert anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only doubting. I was suspicious that it was he who could have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness you presented it as a fact and you even said that he confessed to it, isn't it? That's a fact and not just conclusions. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that he confessed is in the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see anywhere that I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I read it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that if you ask someone whether you explained to General Talic that he had confessed, that if you say, "I conveyed this to General Talic," that -- but let's not, at this moment, argue about that. Did you say at the time what is recorded you to have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About that you said at that time that the colonel was responsible, Brajic was responsible. Is that what you said at the time and not that you had doubts as whether he was but you just presented that for a fact. That's what we read. You agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I agree that he was responsible because he was in direct command of those activities. I tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for one reason or another, you are evading to answer my questions. I just simply asked you whether that is what you had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I again have to -- and I will maybe ask Colonel to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please remove your headphones, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, when somebody says "sumnjao sam" can be translated "I had doubts" and can be translated "I suspected." And I asked translators to verify that, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How I understood, Colonel Basara is telling us he suspected not that he had doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, whether the one is true or the other, what is recorded at this statement that he presents for facts and the question whether he had doubts or whether it was just suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When he had said today that he had doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing we're doing at this moment and it takes us a while to establish whether the witness said in Stanisic and Zupljanin what he is recorded to have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at that time from what we read in the transcript, but it always can be verified if there are serious doubts, we read that he presented that for a fact, and whether today he says it was just a suspicion or I had doubts or whatever, the issue at stake is that he was -- what he presented as a fact in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case is now presented as an uncertainty, and I leave it apart whether that is suspicion or doubt or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, why I intervened that doubt is in your question as well so it might be confusing a bit [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line -- page 56, line 18 so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the problems is, Mr. Lukic, and you certainly are aware of that whatever question you ask the witness he has apparently difficulties in answering that question rather -- but let me see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I should have said, not that it was just a suspicion or that you had doubts. If the two meanings are there -- but again the core issue is whether the witness said so. Now I don't intend to spend more time with the witness on that. As to whether there's any doubt he said that, we'll have to check the Stanisic and Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He admitted that he said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- well, you are optimistic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you can check with him. Because he was talking about burned mosque or destroyed mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I asked him whether he said that the Colonel was responsible he said he was responsible but he didn't do it and -- well, let's -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- let's continue with the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And take a break first. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after this break. We resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the videolink is functioning well, we can continue, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And staying on this topic of Major Brajic and mosques, could we please go back to Colonel Basara's interview in 2002, 65 ter 27986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P7322, reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Mental block. Although there may be -- that's the whole -- yeah, that's fine. Could we please go to page 108 in the English and 138 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version has 137 pages in total. Can counsel check?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English, it's two pages from the end so that may make it easier to find the corresponding B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could back two pages in the B/C/S, please. And back another page as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The top of the page is at the bottom of the B/C/S version: "What could I do?" It's BB from the bottom of the page, if that's what you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd like to go from where we see the question: "Can I ask you one question?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the last question on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, focussing your attention on the bottom of the page, at line 31 and looking at the English at line 6, we see you're asked the following question: "Can I ask you one question? When the Chief of Staff gave the orders for the destruction of the mosque in Mahala, was it actually destroyed?" Your answer: "Yes, it was demolished, and do you know how I came to that conclusion? Because I was not on my command post and the chief -- and the chief engineer wants to see me. And I used a bit of a ruse and I just extended my hand and said: Thank you to you it was really done brightly, and he just laughed and he said: We didn't need much explosive. It just lied down. Because the Chief of Staff had actually told me [sic] that those were my orders, that I had ordered" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry. "Had told him that those were my orders, that I had ordered it, and so he gave himself out and he admitted to having done it. To which - and then I told him, you know: I, I, it wasn't me, I didn't issue the order. You were, basically, you were cheated. They cheated you. And, so you will be the one who will be held responsible for this. And, so one day, if you're held responsible you go and then you tell people at whose orders you actually did this."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, here you are relaying how you -- you tricked your chief engineer into admitting to you that he destroyed the mosque in Mahala upon the orders of Major Brajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the impression you get from reading it. But later on when I learned what I learnt, as I said, I realised it couldn't have been him. He may have been present though because later on he refused to admit it. So as it probably turned out he was there, present but Njunja was the man in charge who set the explosives. The other guy was not as competent to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, you would agree that in 2002, there was no doubt in your mind about who -- who was in charge and who was responsible for the demolition of this mosque in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, and, as I said, I provided that particular answer to that question at the time. But later on, through conversations and when I thought about it carefully, I concluded that the chief of engineers did not have sufficient knowledge to destroy a mosque in one go. Then I realised that it was done by Njunja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He may have been present only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm interrupting you. Could you please answer the questions and refrain from a lot of other comments because the question still was whether in 2002, it was clear on your mind who was in charge and who was responsible for the demolition of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you told, as you said in the beginning of today -- of -- your testimony in this Court, that when you gave your statement, including the one in 2002, that you had told the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, in paragraph 64 of your statement, you say the following: "I do not know who destroyed the mosques in Sanski Most. The perpetrators put stockings on their head." Now, sir, now you're telling the Court that you -- that you learnt that it was Njunja who destroyed this mosque in Mahala. So my question to is why did you not make that clear in your statement and -- and why did you not make clear your previous suspicions about Major Brajic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean -- I don't understand this question very well. When the mosque in Mahala was destroyed, there were no people with stockings on their heads. It had to do with other mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you say in your statement, paragraph 64: "I do not know who destroyed these mosques in Sanski Most. The perpetrators put stockings on their head." And I'm putting to that you do have an idea about who was involved. You once thought it was a Major Brajic. You now seem to be telling us that it was a man called Njunja. So why not mention that in your statement that you've put into evidence before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, when there are 100 ambiguous questions, one often has a slip of the tongue or says something that may not necessarily be so. Now, as you put this question, it doesn't pertain to mosques but a mosque. They had their stockings in Sanski Most on their heads. It doesn't concern mosques, in the plural. In Mahala, there was no one with a stocking on their head. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person to arrive in the area of the mosque was Njunja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm less focussed on stockings on heads and more the fact that you say you have no idea who destroyed the mosques in Sanski Most. Can we agree that when you said that actually it wasn't the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you put such questions that one simply doesn't know how to answer them. No matter what I say seems to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I discussed mosques, in the plural, all mosques, and yet again you go back to a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that single one, Witness, is included in the overall category mosques in Sanski Most. Now, in your statement, you say you had no idea of the perpetrators. Today you told us that, at least in relation to Mahala, you had an idea about the perpetrators, that is, Njunja. And that is what Mr. Jeremy is drawing your attention --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only for one mosque in Mahala. As for the other mosques, I was never able to find out who destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a truthful answer to what you were asked when you gave your statement in paragraph 64 would have been: I do not know who destroyed the mosques in Sanski Most apart from Mahala, where I had an idea who had done it." That would have been the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would have been the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, you -- you know that all the mosques in Sanski Most were knocked down, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether all of them were knocked down. As for the villages I went through, I could see that they were, indeed, destroyed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at your Stanisic and Zupljanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'd like to tender the page of this 2002 interview that we just looked at. I can come back at the end with an excerpt perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to keep matters also short. Witness, could you tell us whether there was any mosque you saw still standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Mosques may have been destroyed even after my departure. In any case, as for the villages I went through, I think there was only one in Kamengrad, an old mosque that had not been destroyed. The new one was though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only one you still saw not being destroyed in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the only one along the route I travelled the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have a couple of final questions on this, Colonel Basara. Now you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case that General Talic, your superior commander, explained to you that Major Brajic was a good senior officer who should be kept. And this is in reference to the conversations that you had with General Talic when you suspected that Major Brajic had destroyed this mosque. Now my question to you is: Who was in the superior command who explained to you or explained to General Talic that Major Brajic was a good superior officer who should be kept?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was present. It was a long time ago. He was an infantry man in any case, with specialist knowledge in combat activities and tactical exercises. Given the fact that he was quite younger than me, I expected that he would take over the brigade, and I tried to introduce him to the job, to test him. However, I realised that he was under somebody's influence and I was afraid that politicians would eventually be able to take over the staff and the brigade. When I realised that I could no longer stay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I interrupt you. The simple question was who was in the superior command who explained to you or explained to General Talic that Major Brajic was a good superior officer who should be kept. Who was it? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, there's evidence in this case that the high command did indeed subsequently take steps in respect of Major Brajic, and these steps are indicated in the military notebook of General Mladic, P364, pages 240 to 244. Now, that entry in that notebook dated the 15th of January, 1996, refers to Major Brajic as a -- or refers to a Lieutenant-Colonel Brajic. Were you aware that Brajic was promoted during the course of the war to lieutenant-colonel from a major?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Because when I left the brigade, while I was in the operations group, I know that he was not promoted and later on I have no idea whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the same entry refers to a Lieutenant-Colonel Brajic being appointed to the school of the Main Staff in 1996. Now, were you aware of that, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he went to Manjaca, to the school centre there because he is very competent for training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave that there and we will move on. I'd like to briefly discuss operations that your units were engaged in Hrustovo, late May/early June 1992. Now you refer to Hrustovo in your statements in -- in paragraph 47. You explain that when the battalion commander headed towards Hrustovo with his units and entered the village two of his soldiers were killed and you explain that the soldiers gave civilians within Hrustovo the opportunity to evacuate before an attack was launched. That's your -- that's -- that's what you say in paragraph 47. Now you also say that it -- individuals that perished in the village were Muslims who had taken part in the fighting against VRS forces in Hrustovo on the 31st of May, 1992 and you say that these Muslim fighters were dressed in civilian clothes and they were not buried with their weapons so that when they are exhumed one would get the impression that they are civilians, and you say that you exclude the possibility that anyone who did not take part in the combat activities was killed there. Now, Colonel Basara, this Chamber has received evidence that Serb soldiers shot dead a number of civilians, overwhelmingly women and children, who were hiding in a garage, the Merdanovic garage, in Hrustovo on the 31st of May, 1992. P2499, for example. Now this evidence includes exhumation reports, for example, P3299. Now, just so I'm clear, you're not suggesting that these persons were somehow Muslim fighters dressed in civilian clothes, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether the evidence this Chamber received that women and children were killed during the Hrustovo event, whether they were -- had taken part in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's clear to everyone that they did not take part in combat. But do give me the day when the first actions took place in Hrustovo and when these people fell victim. So it's not the same day, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, the day is the 31st of May, 1992, and the evidence that this Chamber has received is that women and children were murdered in a garage in Hrustovo on the 31st of May, 1992. Now you were -- you are aware of that incident; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that later. I heard of this incident later. I don't know when exactly when I was being questioned. But do tell me the date, when you have this recorded. When did this first attack take place against Hrustovo? I would like to know that date. You do have it registered, don't you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Basara, I will repeat the date, it's 31st of May 1992, and you are saying that you were aware of the casualties of women and children but you're also saying that you exclude the possibility that anyone who took part in combat activities was killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did not take part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because combat was taking place. Two hours were given so that all of those who did not wish to fight just like I did in Mahala that they could pull out of that village and go towards Sanski Most. Those who stayed, if combat activities were taking place, could have lost his life and, of course, who was fighting could certainly have been killed. So the army did something that I thought was normal. That is to say, those who do not wish to fight should leave. That is to say, those who remain in Hrustovo would be the ones who wished to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel, do you accept that some civilians did remain and those civilians did lose their lives on the 31st of May in Hrustovo in the Merdanovic garage?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that. Those who did not want to get out when combat activities were taking place could have lost his life. When NATO was bombing they didn't give a second for anyone to leave and everybody who got killed was considered to be collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you then consider the killing of women and children in the garage as collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not. But if they did not leave from areas where mortars, Osas, Zoljas and other weapons were being fired then it could have happened that they would get killed. Nobody could have stopped that from happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it your information that they were killed from mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because according to some statements, it says artillery was fired in Hrustovo for three days. So from the area of Golaja, Muslims were firing mortars against the Serbs when they entered Hrustovo. So they could have been killed by their shells too. And before they entered the village, it could have been ours too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not know, really, about how they were killed? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your statement, where you say, "I exclude the possibility that anyone who did not take part in the combat activities was killed there," as a matter of fact, you do not know that either, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just know that those who did not leave Hrustovo could have lost their lives, and I do not know of a single one who had been killed that had not been fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including those women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already told you about the women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How that could happen ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, the women and children in this garage the evidence that this Chamber has received is that they were not killed by shells or Zoljas that they were killed by weapons, automatic weapons being fired into the garage in which they were hiding. But you indicated that you don't have clear knowledge about this, but that do you know that your units were in Hrustovo village on the 31st of May, 1992, that's -- that's accurate, yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the 31st of May because I did not keep a diary or something. I don't know what date it was. I don't know that now. And I do know that activities evolved in the way in which I have already presented. As for the dates you have there I mean, there are different references to different dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you're very clear on dates in your statement which is what I'm using now. Let's move onto Vrhpolje which as I understand it was a related operation and which you discuss in your statements. Now, citizen -- civilians who were evacuating from Hrustovo or all those people who didn't want to fight in Hrustovo headed towards Vrhpolje. That's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So they were going as they were retreating gradually, nobody took them out. They, themselves, went towards Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, so the answer is yes. In paragraph 42 of your statement you discuss what you call the crime at Vrhpolje bridge where 16 Muslims were killed took place on that same day, and --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So that you're aware that the Prosecution charges that there were 28 persons that day, but I want to discuss these events now. Now, your position is that persons who were evacuated from Hrustovo were murdered on Vrhpolje bridge by paramilitaries who intercepted them and then executed a number of them on that bridge. That's -- that's basically your position; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is not several of them as you had put it, but it's 16. That is the group that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we could not establish who they were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood, Colonel, and I'm sorry to speak across you, I have limited time. Now, there's evidence before this Trial Chamber and that's at T147 to T169 that the men executed on the bridge of Vrhpolje were being escorted out of Hrustovo by your soldiers who then executed the men on that bridge. And that's -- that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the truth. That is a total fabrication of those who are now providing you with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's go through that in a little bit of detail. Now, from your statement, you indicate that you actually heard the firing on the bridge that -- when you were 100 or 200 metres away from the bridge. This is paragraph 43. Now, It's correct that there was a civilian police check-point on or very near to Vrhpolje bridge; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not civilian police but armed men. Some had blue uniforms, I mean, of the civilian protection, others had these camouflage uniforms. Now they were -- was it from the Territorial Defence or civilian protection from Sanski Most? They were the ones who held the check-point there, right by the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So there was a check-point by the bridge which -- which you say may have been staffed by men in blue uniforms or camouflage uniforms. Now you previously indicated that the men at that check-point were armed. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were armed, and they fired and they made these other people jump into the Sana and then they fired at them. That's the information that I received from these people who watched that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel, to be clear, I want to draw a distinction between the people who you believe are responsible for the executions on the bridge and the people who were staffing the check-point that was on or near to the bridge which you've previously discussed. Now you previously indicated there was a civilian police check-point, that was in the close vicinity of the bridge. So is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that this did exist but it didn't have to be the civilian police. I knew that these were people who were appointed by the leadership of Sanski Most. Now whether there were policemen among them and who that was, that I don't know. But they were at that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Are you now saying today that it was people who were at that check-point who were also involved in the executions on Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not involved. They were in shelters when I jumped out of the vehicle and ran towards the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And these men who were in the shelters, they were -- they were armed but they took no steps to prevent the executions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did not expect that to happen at all. Because that happened in a moment, so they could not react at all. They couldn't have prevented that. The order issued was that these people should jump and they did not expect them to shoot at them and this happened at lightning speed. And I checked that, and they said that could have not have intervened at all. And then this group escaped to the other side of the bridge when they heard them shouting, Colonel Basara. Then they ran away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, can I ask one clarifying question. You said the order issued was that these people should jump. How do you know that this was the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen, now you'll be asking me whether it was written too. Well, the group that was shooting ordered them. They demanded that they jump into the water. And then we jumped into the water, then they started firing at them. And the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I stop you there. First of all, would you refrain from cynical observations. Second, would you please answer my question. My question was: How did you know that this was the order issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you have to explain to me who issued the order so that I could answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was it that could have issued the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I took it from your statement that those who -- Witness, would you not interrupt me. I took it -- Witness, do not interrupt me. Otherwise we'll have to deal with it in another way. I took from your statement that those on the bridge who killed the soldiers, that they ordered them to jump from that bridge. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's it. Now who ordered that, they ordered that, and those people jumped in, and then they fired at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my question is: How do you know that they were ordered to jump from the bridge instead of, for example, being kicked from the bridge or whatever, but how do you know that they were ordered to jump from that bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no other way they could have jumped, when these people at the check-point claim that they did not throw them in or push them in or that. They said that all of a sudden they all jumped from the bridge. So the only thing that could have happened was that somebody had ordered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we are clearly separating the people at the check-point who were in the shelter and those were at the bridge. I'm focussing at this moment on those on the bridge. You said they ordered them to jump from that bridge. Now, could you tell us, how do you know that it -- they ordered them to do that or that they spontaneously jumped from the bridge, or that they were kicked from the bridge, or whatever may have happened? How do you know that they were ordered to jump from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the explanation given to me was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, in respect to this incident in paragraph 43 of your statement, you say that no one recognised the perpetrators. Now, you -- you don't mention this in your statement --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the fact is that you recognised two of the people who were on the bridge while the shooting was takes place, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two persons who escorted Major Brajic, they were present by the bridge, but they kept saying to me all the time that they didn't know anybody from that group. And my impression was that they were not firing at all. They had their weapons on their right shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what were the names of these two men who were on the bridge who were Major Brajic's escorts and who had their weapons on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one was Mutic, that was his last name. And the other one's first name is Ilija but I don't have all their details. It was a long time ago. So I just remember that one of the escorts was nicknamed Muta, his last name being Mutic and the other one's first name was Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You previously indicated you thought it might be an Ilija Maksimovic. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Maksimovic, but I don't remember exactly. I just know it is Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now the fact that you recognised two men, two men who were in your brigade who were on the bridge at the time of this execution, did you consider that something relevant to include in your statement? And why didn't you include it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me. And even now, if you're not asking me about something, I don't say anything to you. So if I'm not asked, I cannot state anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, these two escorts of Major Brajic who were on this bridge who you spoke to immediately after this incident, you didn't arrest them, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no grounds on which I could have arrested them because when I jumped out of the vehicle, I saw that their weapons were on their shoulders. They were not among those people on the bridge who were fighting, and the group fled, and they just went on standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then they walked up to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the weapons on their shoulders. Did you take those weapons for any sort of ballistics analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I don't want to sound funny now or anything. I didn't send it off for an analysis. I didn't have time to do that, to examine the victims, to send weapons off to ballistics analysis and so on. All the people I had available were reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So 16 men killed almost in front of your eyes and you don't have time to launch a proper investigation into that. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't have time. But I didn't have the experts, the organs who could have done that. And I'm not a professional. I am not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that means that during the war, I should have dealt with such questions, investigations for 90 per cent of my time and leave aside everything else. And combat was ongoing in Hrustovo, so there wasn't enough time. There weren't any professional personnel there who would be capable of doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to make the last session not too short, as a matter of fact, I would refer to take the break now and then resume at quarter to 2.00. Witness, we'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The videolink apparently is still functioning well. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed. If I -- my calculation is okay, then you have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, staying with events on Vrhpolje bridge, there is evidence in this case that a 6th Brigade member, Jadranko Palija, was a perpetrator of the killings on Vrhpolje bridge. That's P7072. Now, Colonel Basara, you knew Jadranko Palija; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, he was convicted for his involvement in these crimes in the State Court of Bosnia. Did you hear about this conviction? And this was in 2008.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he's actually also mentioned in connection with this particular crime in the indictment against you in the State Court that's been issued by the BiH prosecutor, and that's in paragraph 8. Do you recall seeing his name in your indictment. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention to the individual names in the indictment, but I understood the charges as laid out, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at a document that you issued the day after the events on Vrhpolje bridge and the events in Hrustovo, and that's P2366.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could please see that on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a document from the Command of the 6th Brigade and it's dated the 1st of June 1992. If we can please go to page 3 in the English and the B/C/S. Sorry, page 2 in the B/C/S, the last page. And we see your name and the signature. Is that your signature, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the paragraph immediately above your signature, we read that: This order shall be read out to all subordinate units of the brigade by a time we can't -- that we don't know on the 3rd of June, 1992 and the brigade command is to be informed about it through the regular communications system. Colonel Basara, you said something that wasn't captured, could you -- could you repeat it. Or are you saying yes, yes it is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, the date is 3rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now if we go back to the first page of this document, please. And the heading is "Establishing discipline in the units of the brigade during combat operations." And we see that there is an order and there are a number of items - we don't have time to deal with them all - but I'd like to focus your attention on -- on number 2. So we see that: "In future combat operations we must not repeat the mistakes we've made before in the treatment of prisoners and that no one has the right to beat or abuse prisoners when they are brought in and until questioning has been carried out. Any soldier who abuses prisoners must be discharged from the unit without delay." And then number 3: "I categorically forbid acts of genocide against the population of the opposing side who are unable to fight, including women, children under 18, the sick and people over 60 years of age." Now, Colonel Basara, this is issued the day after the events in Hrustovo, the -- the executions in the garage. This is a reference to those events, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, I don't know whether it pertained to those events, but it mostly concerned the situation at the Vrhpolje bridge and Kenjari, where 17 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what prompted me to draft this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My understanding is that victims of those events were male, male civilians. Now here we see there's a reference to women and children under 18. So which women and children under 18 did you have in mind when you forbidded [sic] acts of genocide against them on the 3rd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a general formulation. It involved the categories that were supposed to be protected in times of war. That is why it had been ordered that all those not wishing to fight had to withdraw to certain areas. It referred to all those who were not capable of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But when I look at this order, Colonel Basara, and I see the title, "Establishing discipline in the units of the brigade," and I see you forbidding acts of genocide against women and children, that certainly suggests to me that are acts that had been carried out that you now needed to forbid in the future.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be. I always tried to foresee and to take measures to prevent things from happening. As regards your interpretation, I cannot offer any other explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly you're thinking that this -- this could have been an order that you issued in anticipation of any soldiers in your unit thinking about committing genocide against women and children under 18 and you're just simply forbidding any such future activity? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one short question. And, please, a short answer, Witness. The events we discussed earlier, did they play any role in triggering you to issue this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to a certain extent, especially the event at the Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It - how should I put it? - it completely ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, you said: "It completely ..." and then I didn't hear the remainder of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I put it? It drove me nuts completely, thinking that people could do such a thing. I was concerned that such a situation could repeat -- be repeated. That is why I issued this order to pre-empt any such future events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was it then your own soldiers who had done it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't done by my soldiers. But one learns from others' mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to understand why you said that you wanted to -- to restore or at least heighten the discipline. It was triggered by these events, you were addressing your own soldiers, although the events were not including anything done by your soldiers. I'm trying to understand that. If you would be in a position to give me one or two more words on it, I would appreciate it. Next question, please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, just before we leave this document, I'd like to focus your attention on number 1 and the third bullet point down where we see a reference to: "All soldiers prone to burning down and destroying buildings from which the enemy is not opening fire at the unit must be discharged." Now, at the time, you -- you believed that -- or -- that Major Brajic had destroyed the mosque in Mahala but you -- you -- you didn't discharge your Chief of Staff from your unit in -- pursuant to your own order, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't prove that. I had no witnesses, and I couldn't have him removed on the basis of my suspicion. It is also a question of whether my superior command in the corps would have allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you think that your superior command in the corps wouldn't have allowed it. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let move on --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was my reasoning at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's move on. In paragraph 50 of your statement, you refer to Skrljevita, and you state that: "I do not even know where this is." The paramilitary would go from municipality to municipality and that your unit was not in that village. Now, Colonel Basara, it's -- it's -- it's correct that you actually issued a criminal report against Danilusko Kajtez in respect of this incident on the 7th of December, 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is incorrect. It was issued by Colonel Kajtez, his uncle, because it happened after I left the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a quick look at 65 ter 06529, please. Now, on the screen before you, Colonel Basara, is a document dated the 7th of December, 1992. You'd not left the brigade by this time, correct, you said you left in the middle of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when I left, but it was sometime in December. You have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's go to the last page. And we see there, Colonel Basara, your name and your signature. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we go to page 2 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S, please. Now, Colonel Basara, you see that the subheading, "Description of crime." We see that on the 1st of November, 1992, in Glamosnica, the passage for Skrljevita, Danilusko Kajtez and others laid in wait for a man who came from Skrljevita who Dane then" - if we go to the next page in the English - "questioned about who was on guard, what weapons they had, who was organising them. Dane then killed with him his light machine-gun by firing a bullet into his chest." And then you go on to talk about another incident on -- on the same day, where more persons were killed. So I understand it was a long time ago, Colonel Basara, but in fact, you did know about this incident in Skrljevita and you did have the capacity to request -- request the Office of the Military Prosecutor to investigate certain crimes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It does not say that it was in Skrljevita. Please read the first sentence after the subtitle. It says: "In the place of Glamosnica, passage to Skrljevita." So it's not Skrljevita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Jeremy said Glamosnica and then he ... let me just see. Glamosnica, the palm of Skrljevita. Let me just see whether that's a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In line 17, says this incident in Skrljevita. So it can be [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's -- Yes, apparently the witness -- Mr. Jeremy considered Glamosnica part of that. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah that's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct. That's [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a -- Mr. Lukic, doesn't assist that much, is it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, back to my question. The fact is you did know about this incident in Skrljevita, or near Glamosnica, and that you -- you did request an investigation into this incident by the Office of the Military Prosecutor, and you clearly had the capacity to do that; yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this Danilusko was finally convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir that's not my investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... had been an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please be so kind to answer the question rather than to elaborate on matters not asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, that question is that you did know about these incidents involving Danilusko Kajtez in Skrljevita, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say now that I remember it. However, given the fact that I signed it, in all likelihood information was provided to me by the security organ and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However based on some further --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you would agree that you clearly had the capacity to request the Office of the Military Investigator to investigate crimes that you wanted to be investigated; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was that possibility, and procedure was initiated and information forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 06529 receives number P7323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, a final topic. Now, yesterday you -- you told this Trial Chamber that you had no occasion to meet General Mladic during the war; is that -- is that correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, did you ever attend any meetings at which General Mladic was also present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once, in Banja Luka. There was a large room where many of us were, and Mladic was in attendance. However, I had no opportunity to contact him or to speak with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at a document in connection with that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 00585.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Colonel Basara, what was the -- what was the date of this meeting that you -- you attended together with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No clue. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood. Now on the screen before us we have a report that if we go to the last page or it's dated 16 September 1992. And on the last page we see your signature Commander Colonel Branko Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now we see that this is a report from the consultation on the state of the VRS under the leadership of lieutenant-general Ratko Mladic, and we see reference to a consultation meeting on 13th of September 1992 with -- that included commanders of the brigades in the 1st Krajina Corps. That's the meeting that you recollect; yes? Just a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But without documents to jog my memory I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We have a document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2, please, in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I just want to focus your attention on number 5: Tasks issued by General Mladic. And I'd look to focus just on one of those tasks, number 5 which reads: "Extend maximum support to the civilian authorities and the MUP." Now, Colonel Basara, we see at the start of your testimony that the document that transferred, the order that transferred the 6th Brigade to Sanski Most by General Talic dated the 3rd of April 1992 requested that your brigade establish full co-operation with organs of government in Sanski Most. Now, we see that a number of months on, after the crimes that we have been discussing today, yesterday, and in your statement, you are, again, being advised by General Mladic to extend maximum support to the civilian authorities and the MUP. And that's exactly what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have to refer specifically to what kind of assistance it relates to. Because if they asked for assistance, it was given. If they did not, we did not offer our services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Basara. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, may I take it, not today, but that you would have further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a time estimate for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment. I will be more organised in the morning. But I will have a quite a lot of more questions after this long cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would give us a time estimate tomorrow morning, then we'll consider how much time you'd have. Witness, Mr. Basara, tomorrow, there will be some further questions for you. I hope that all the transportation problems have been resolved. At least I established that you were in the videolink room. I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony given yesterday and today, or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear to you, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. Then we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can close the videolink. I have one short matter which I would like to briefly address. It is about the time available for the Prosecution for presentation of its re-opened case. Last week the Chamber decided on the Prosecution's 45th Rule 92 bis motion. The Chamber is now in a position to set the time available for the Prosecution to present its re-opening. The Prosecution will call eight witnesses - two 92 ter and six expert witnesses - and the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request to hear those eight witnesses within nine hours. We adjourn for the day -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm reminded that I had not yet -- that the Chamber had not yet decided on the admission of the document last tendered by the Prosecution. That was -- yes, that's ... P7324 is admitted into evidence. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 22nd of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of April, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
